prompt: File intake: match each signature result to the suitable handling.

pairs.item: Signature matches the claimed file family
pairs.match: Continue with structural parsing and policy checks

pairs.item: Signature conflicts with the claimed type
pairs.match: Hold, reject or quarantine under documented policy and record the reason
Keep the result unknown and route it for further inspection

explanation: A known signature match is not a full safety check; an unknown signature is uncertainty, not proof of malware.

prompt: An uploaded .docx whose first bytes match the ZIP signature has been confirmed as a valid document.
explanation: A DOCX is a ZIP container, so the ZIP signature alone does not show it is a sound document. A parser checks the structure.

prompt: Secure file intake uses several checks. Match each check to what it tells you.

pairs.match: What type the uploader claims the file is
Whether the first bytes match a known format
Whether the file's internal structure is valid
Whether the bytes match a trusted baseline

explanation: No single check is a full safety test. Log the decision and reason so an analyst can reconstruct the intake result later.

prompt: What does a SHA-256 mismatch against a trusted baseline establish?

options.text: The file’s bytes differ from that baseline
Which user account last changed the file
options.why: A hash compares bytes only; it records nothing about who made a change.

options.text: The time at which the file was last changed
options.why: A hash has no time information; it can't tell you when a change happened.

options.text: That the file has been infected with malware
options.why: Legitimate edits also change the hash; a mismatch shows difference, not infection.

explanation: The hash alone does not identify the person, time or reason. The baseline and its source must be trustworthy.

prompt: You expected a process-creation event in the Security log, but none is present. Which of these could explain the missing event? Select all that apply.

options.text: Process-creation auditing was not enabled
Older records were overwritten under retention settings
You lack permission to read the Security log
The process definitely never ran
options.why: A missing event describes the log, not reality; the process may have run without being recorded.

options.text: Event Viewer always records every action
options.why: Event Viewer only shows what auditing captured and retention kept.

explanation: "No event found" describes this collection. It is not proof an action never happened.

prompt: Match each Registry location to what it holds.

pairs.match: Values that can start programs at sign-in
pairs.why: Run keys make programs start at sign-in.

explanation: Run keys are a common place for software, legitimate or not, to make itself start automatically.

prompt: A Windows record shows a particular USB storage device was connected to a laptop. What can that record support on its own?

options.text: That a device with that identifier was connected
That a specific file was copied onto the device
options.why: Connecting a device doesn't show any particular file was copied.

options.text: That company data was taken off the laptop by someone
options.why: A connection record alone doesn't show data left the laptop.

options.text: The exact time of every later connection of the device
options.why: Device records don't list the exact time of every later connection.

explanation: Device history shows a device was seen. Correlate it with file-access, process and transfer records before claiming anything was copied.

prompt: Put these steps for analysing a security signal in order.
steps: Observe: cite the exact file, event, account, path, source and UTC time
Interpret: state a hypothesis and why the combination is unusual
Test: check an independent source such as process, file or network evidence
explanation: Scripts make the first pass repeatable; the analyst still owns the conclusion.

prompt: 10:14 to 10:16 three failed network logons; 10:18 the same account and source succeeds; 10:21 a new startup entry; 10:24 a new USB device. What is the most defensible conclusion?

options.text: It warrants investigation, but proves neither malware nor data loss
Malware was installed and data was then copied to the USB device
options.why: The sequence is suspicious, but nothing here shows malware ran or data was copied.

options.text: It was a brute-force attack, followed by exfiltration of data to USB
options.why: Failed then successful logons and a USB device fit an attack, but also innocent explanations.

options.text: The events are unrelated and normal, so no follow-up is needed
options.why: The combination is unusual enough to check; dismissing it risks missing a real incident.

explanation: Record exact entries, consider benign explanations, and identify the next record that could distinguish them.

prompt: Which fields should an application audit log record? Select all that apply.

options.text: An unambiguous UTC time
The action and outcome
The resource affected
A correlation or request ID
The submitted password
options.why: Logging passwords creates a new store of secrets that anyone with log access can read.

options.text: The user's session token
options.why: A session token in a log lets anyone who reads the log act as that user.

explanation: Logs should help reconstruct events while avoiding passwords, session tokens and unnecessary personal data.

prompt: An unfamiliar value under a Run key is a reason to investigate, not proof that malware is present.
explanation: Legitimate software also uses Run keys. Investigate the path, signature, hash, signer, process telemetry and approved baseline.

prompt: A Run key value exists on the machine today. What do you need before calling it "new"?

options.text: An earlier trusted snapshot to compare it with
Nothing, since the value itself records when it was added
options.why: A Registry value doesn't record when it was first added.

options.text: A failed-logon event from around the same time
options.why: A failed logon doesn't tell you whether a Run key value is new.

options.text: The file extension of the program the value launches
options.why: The launched program's extension says nothing about when the value appeared.

explanation: A current value does not say when it first appeared.

prompt: What should you do before sorting records from different systems into a timeline?

options.text: Convert all timestamps to UTC and note their source
Use each computer's local display time exactly as shown
options.why: Local display times use different time zones and settings, so they can't be sorted together.

options.text: Use the time the evidence was extracted as the event time
options.why: When evidence was extracted is not when the original event happened.

options.text: Discard any records that don't include an event ID number
options.why: Records without an event ID can still be important evidence.

explanation: Extraction time, file display time or a local clock is not automatically the time of the event.

prompt: Why record a timestamp's original value and offset as well as the converted UTC time?

options.text: So anyone can check the conversion against the time as it was recorded
Because UTC times are less precise than the original local times
options.why: UTC is just as precise; the point is preserving the original evidence.

options.text: Because local times sort more reliably when building a timeline
options.why: UTC is what you sort by; local times with different offsets sort badly.

options.text: It is only needed when the evidence is going to be used in court
options.why: Keeping the original matters for any analysis, not only court cases.

explanation: Normalise before sorting, but keep the time as recorded and note clock uncertainty and source.

prompt: A user uploads invoice.pdf, but its first bytes match the ZIP signature. What should the service do?

options.text: Hold or reject it under policy and record why
Accept it, because the .pdf extension says it is a PDF
options.why: The extension is a claim from the uploader; the bytes say otherwise.

options.text: Rename it to .zip so the type matches, then accept it
options.why: Renaming to match hides the conflict instead of handling it under policy.

options.text: Label it as malware and report the user to security
options.why: A type mismatch is a reason to hold the file, not proof it's malware or that the user is malicious.

explanation: The extension is a user-supplied claim. A conflict between claimed type and signature is a reason to hold, not proof of malice.

prompt: If a file's signature is not recognised, the file should be treated as malware.
explanation: An unknown signature is uncertainty. Keep the result unknown and route it for further inspection rather than guessing.

prompt: Several failed logons are followed by a successful logon for the same account. What does this show on its own?

options.text: Worth investigating, though it could just be someone mistyping a password
A confirmed brute-force attack that has compromised the account
options.why: A success after failures is consistent with an attack, but also with someone mistyping.

options.text: That malware is running on the machine and guessing passwords
options.why: Failed logons don't show malware; people mistype passwords all the time.

options.text: Nothing worth recording, since failed logons are very common
options.why: A run of failures followed by success is worth recording and checking.

explanation: Observe, interpret, then test against an independent source such as process, endpoint or network evidence.
